To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

HIV/HBV and HIV/HCV coinfection is a major issue in the context of the HIV/AIDS epidemic, that the management of these coinfections has changed in the last few years and that the challenge for the future is to ensure access to optimal treatment for both infections.

the prevalence of HBV and especially HCV coinfection is still very high, with a significant negative impact on morbidity and mortality, and that the new era of direct-acting antivirals has completely changed our management of HCV infection.
HIV and hepatitis coinfection are still frequent, and the liver is a major target of both viruses.

a comprehensive understanding of the impact of HIV coinfection on the natural history of chronic viral hepatitis in the liver and the development of new therapeutic strategies for the management of chronic hepatitis in HIV infected patients, with a particular emphasis on the use of direct acting antivirals in HIV/HCV coinfection and the management of HBV low replicating viremia.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV/HCV or HIV/HBV coinfection is a complex, multifactorial and evolving disease that requires the expertise of a multidisciplinary team to provide the best clinical management to patients.

, although the management of HBV and, especially, HCV coinfection in HIV patients has improved in the last decade, there are still many challenges to face, especially in terms of accessibility to new therapies and their integration with antiretroviral therapy.
HIV and viral hepatitis coinfection is a field of great complexity that is constantly evolving.

coinfection is a major challenge for the HIV community and a field of research and care that is still in progress.
the management of HBV and/or HCV coinfections has changed dramatically in the last years.

the current challenge in the management of HBV and/or HCV coinfection in HIV is the need for a multidisciplinary approach and for a closer collaboration between hepatology and infectious diseases specialists.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HIV coinfection with HBV or HCV is a complex and challenging field of research and clinical practice that should be managed in specialised centres, with the aim to improve patient care and outcomes.
the management of HIV/HBV or HIV/HCV coinfection has become more complex than ever and requires a multidisciplinary approach.
the management of chronic hepatitis in the context of coinfection with HIV is a complex issue, which should ideally be managed in a specialised setting.
